intro: Jascha Heifetz plays the Chaconne, the long final movement of Bach’s Partita No. 2 in D minor, BWV 1004. The solo violin moves from broad chords to fast runs, modulates to D major, and ends on the D-minor chord with which it began.

sections.label: A · D-minor chords and variations
sections.mNote: The violin varies a four-bar harmonic pattern.

sections.label: Dev · Chords broken across the strings
sections.mNote: Arpeggios spread the harmony into a continuous line.

sections.label: B · D major and low chords
sections.mNote: F♯ replaces F♮ in the central variations.

sections.label: C · D minor returns
sections.mNote: Fresh variations follow the return of F♮

sections.label: A′ · The opening chords again
sections.mNote: The first dotted rhythm returns before the final D

cues.title: Opening chord and four-bar pattern
cues.text: The violin begins with a D-minor chord and a dotted rhythm, entering on the second beat of the bar. Bass and melody sound together. Over the next four bars Bach sets out the harmonies for the succession of variations that follows.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1879), Chaconne, opening four-bar pattern and two-beat opening bar. Mutopia edition: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=1426.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Manuscript of six works, 1720
cues.text: Bach gathered three sonatas and three partitas for solo violin in a manuscript dated 1720. In this partita the Ciaccona is the fifth and final movement, after an Allemande, Courante, Sarabande and Gigue.
cues.evidence: Autograph date and movement order: Netherlands Bach Society, https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-1004. The manuscript date is distinct from the date of composition.

cues.title: Death of Maria Barbara, 1720
cues.text: When Bach returned from Carlsbad with Prince Leopold in 1720, he learned that his wife, Maria Barbara, had died after a short illness and had already been buried. Since 1994 the scholar Helga Thoene has argued that the Chaconne is her epitaph. The idea is disputed, and Bach left no word on it.
cues.evidence: Maria Barbara’s death and burial during Bach’s absence in 1720: Bach-Archiv Leipzig, chronology, https://www.bach-leipzig.de/en/neutral/johann-sebastian-bach-%E2%94%80-chronology. Helga Thoene’s 1994 article arguing that the Chaconne is a tombeau for her, “a deeply controversial article”: Michael Spitzer, editorial, Eighteenth-Century Music 19/1 (2022), 5–12, https://doi.org/10.1017/S1478570621000324. Her reading underlies the ECM recording Morimur: https://ecmrecords.com/product/morimur-christoph-poppen-the-hilliard-ensemble/

cues.title: Letter to Clara Schumann, 1877
cues.text: In June 1877 Brahms wrote to Clara Schumann: “On a single stave, for a small instrument, the man writes a whole world of the deepest thoughts and most powerful feelings.” He sent her his version of the Chaconne for piano, left hand alone.
cues.evidence: Brahms to Clara Schumann, Pörtschach, late June 1877; Litzmann, correspondence, vol. 2, pp. 111–112. Our translation of the German quoted in Valerie Woodring Goertzen’s Henle preface: https://www.henle.de/media/ec/91/f8/1697725831/1187-1697725831-sync.pdf

cues.title: Arpeggio passage
cues.text: Bach wrote arpeggio above the chords. The player breaks them into a running pattern across the strings, with a bass note below and a melody at the top. The middle notes move between them.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1879), Chaconne, bars 89–120: arpeggio marking and chordal notation. Mutopia edition, music ID 1426.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: L’Enfant Plaza Metro, Washington, 2007
cues.text: At 7:51 on the morning of 12 January 2007 the violinist Joshua Bell, wearing a baseball cap, began with this Chaconne at L’Enfant Plaza Metro station in Washington. In 43 minutes 1,097 people passed. Seven stopped to listen, and 27 left about $32 between them.
cues.evidence: Gene Weingarten, “Pearls Before Breakfast”, The Washington Post, 8 April 2007 (archived copy: https://web.archive.org/web/2007/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2007/04/04/AR2007040401721_pf.html): Bell “decided to begin with ‘Chaconne’”; 1,097 passers-by in 43 minutes; seven stopped; 27 gave $32 and change.

cues.title: Change to D major, bars 133–140
cues.text: After a long span in the minor, F♯ enters and the violin moves into D major at bar 133. The dotted rhythm continues, with the melody placed low on the instrument.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1879), Chaconne, bars 133–140: change to D major and lower melodic writing. Mutopia edition, music ID 1426.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Heifetz recording, RCA 45, 1952
cues.text: This Chaconne comes from a Jascha Heifetz recording issued on an RCA 45-rpm disc, ERA 9544, recorded in 1952. The two sides of the disc are joined here into one track, with no break at the side change.
cues.evidence: Internet Archive item description: “17 cm Single RCA ERA 9544 (2 sides, here put together) … rec. 1952”. https://archive.org/details/chaconne-d-moll-heifetz

cues.title: Chordal writing, bars 177–184
cues.text: Broad dotted phrases return in the section in D major. After pages of quick single notes, the violin plays chords again. The upper line descends through a chain of appoggiaturas, each resolving into the next chord.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1879), Chaconne, bars 177–184: chordal writing and descending melodic pairs. Mutopia edition, music ID 1426.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Bach as violinist, Weimar, 1703
cues.text: In 1703 the eighteen-year-old Bach spent about half a year as a violinist in Duke Johann Ernst III’s private orchestra at Weimar. Seventeen years later he dated a manuscript of six works for solo violin, and ended the D-minor Partita with this Chaconne.
cues.evidence: Bach-Archiv Leipzig, chronology, entry for 1703: https://www.bach-leipzig.de/en/neutral/johann-sebastian-bach-%E2%94%80-chronology. The 1720 manuscript: Netherlands Bach Society, https://www.bachvereniging.nl/en/bwv/bwv-1004.

cues.title: Return to D minor, bar 209
cues.text: At bar 209 F♮ returns and the music moves from D major back to D minor. The violin starts a new group of variations and soon breaks its chords into quick lines again. The opening theme returns once more later.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1879), Chaconne, bar 209 onwards: return to D minor. Mutopia edition, music ID 1426.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Return of the opening chords
cues.text: A last run of notes ends on D. The dotted rhythm of the opening returns, with its broad chords and upper A. Eight bars take the violin to the final D, held under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1879), Chaconne, bars 249–257: opening rhythm restored and final fermata. Mutopia edition, music ID 1426.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: D minor spread across the strings
transitions.to: Dev · Chords broken across the strings
transitions.how: The quick descending line reaches a D-minor chord. Bach marks the following chords arpeggio, and the bow distributes their notes across the strings. The bass and the upper melody stay at the outer edges of the pattern, and the inner notes move between them.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1879), Chaconne, bars 88–93; Mutopia edition, music ID 1426.

transitions.title: The turn to D major
transitions.from: Dev · Chords broken across the strings
transitions.to: B · D major and low chords
transitions.how: The minor-key variations close on D. At bar 133 the key signature changes to D major. The next phrase keeps D as its centre and adds F♯, the major third. The violin begins a lower, dotted melody in D major, with notes sounded beneath it on the other strings.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1879), Chaconne, bars 129–140; D-major key signature at bar 133. Mutopia edition, music ID 1426.

transitions.title: F♮ brings back D minor
transitions.from: B · D major and low chords
transitions.how: The major section closes on D. F♮ returns in the next chord, and the violin begins another set of variations in D minor. The bass stays on D at the join, and the upper line starts a new dotted phrase.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1879), Chaconne, bars 208–213; return to the minor key signature at bar 209. Mutopia edition, music ID 1426.

transitions.title: The opening dotted rhythm returns
transitions.how: The violin’s last rapid run ends on D and pauses. The opening dotted rhythm returns on the second beat, with the D-minor chords and the upper A. A final extension of that phrase leads to the held D under the closing fermata.
transitions.evidence: Bach-Gesellschaft score (1879), Chaconne, bars 248–257; Mutopia edition, music ID 1426.

composer.epithet: Composer who supplied music for Leipzig’s churches for twenty-seven years and wrote a large body of keyboard music.
facts: His brother Johann Christoph in Ohrdruf; St Michael’s School, Lüneburg
Organist, teacher, cantor and director of Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum
Cantatas and Passions; organ and keyboard collections; concertos and solo string music
composer.background:
Bach grew up in a house full of working musicians. His father, Johann Ambrosius, served the town of Eisenach; apprentices lived with the family, and relatives held church and civic posts across Thuringia. Johann Sebastian was born in 1685. His mother died when he was nine, his father the following year, and he moved to Ohrdruf to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist taught by Pachelbel. He sang in the school choir and learnt the organ at home. At fifteen he went to St Michael’s School in Lüneburg, where his voice helped pay for his education. In 2006 some of his schoolboy copies of north German organ works, including two of the hardest pieces of the day, were found in the Anna Amalia Library in Weimar.

In 1702 he won the organist’s post at Sangerhausen, until the duke intervened and gave it to someone else. The next year Arnstadt hired him to examine its new organ and then to play it. Two years later he set off on foot to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck. He stayed for months, far beyond his authorised leave, and came back to a reprimand. In 1707 he moved to Mühlhausen and on 17 October married his second cousin Maria Barbara at Dornheim. The cantata for the inauguration of Mühlhausen’s town council in February 1708, Gott ist mein König, BWV 71, was one of the few works printed in his lifetime. In his cantata Aus der Tiefen, BWV 131, one voice sings the psalmist’s plea while another sings a hymn in long notes above it.
